title: The Input Layer: Prompt Engineering Isn't Dead. You're Just Doing It Wrong.
author: Zack Shapiro

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supplies evidence relevant to the synthesis—especially Harvey’s rapid commercial growth and the continuing duty of lawyers to review AI-generated work—but it is a set of reference notes rather than a developed argument. It does not take a discernible position on agentic infrastructure, vertical-vendor durability, workflow redesign, or the tool-versus-service divide.
qs: 2026): Justice Linda Kevins found defense counsel violated Rules 1.1, 1.3, and 3.1 for submitting AI-generated filings without meaningful review, cautioning that lawyers “may not abdicate these core professional responsibilities to an AI platform.” New York Commercial Division Practice (February 2026).
ARR reached $190M by end of 2025, nearly doubling from $100M five months earlier.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source documents reported hallucination incidents, contested litigation allegations and law-firm reprimands, which is consistent with the cluster’s account of concrete legal risks. However, it does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal governance proposition: that sanctions should target deficient human inquiry while broad verification and human accountability remain controlling amid disagreement over AI-specific rules.
qs: AI hallucination cases in legal filings: As of early 2026, publicly reported cases exceeded 550 nationwide.

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The source accepts the need for governance by framing instruction–intent gaps as an alignment problem and adds concrete evidence of fabricated-citation incidents and law-firm reprimands. This materially strengthens the cluster’s account of verification-related risk, while not addressing insurance coverage, pricing or whether coverage can substitute for professional duties.
qs: The gap between instruction and intent is not merely a prompting inconvenience.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s claim that legal procedure and matter context—not finished templates alone—are the key source of differentiation. It explains what must be encoded, including sequencing, analytical frameworks and judgment calls, while its evidence remains experiential and does not establish autonomous practice or specialist-vendor displacement.
qs: It’s a detailed operating procedure for how the output gets created: decision trees, analytical frameworks, sequencing logic, edge-case handling, judgment calls about when to be aggressive and when to hold back.
You don’t get at what makes a great contract lawyer great by training on thousands of that lawyer’s (or firm’s) contracts.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Shapiro accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and materially develops it by identifying the “input layer” as a key implementation mechanism: professionals must perform the substantive analysis, encode matter-specific context and judgment into instructions, and then verify AI-assisted execution. His account adds concrete detail on interaction and workflow design, though its broad claims rest mainly on practice experience and illustrative incidents rather than controlled evidence.
qs: There’s another possibility that he doesn’t consider: you do the hard thinking first, all of it, the planning, the analysis, the strategy, the judgment, and then you bring in the AI to execute on that thinking, or to pressure-test it, or to help you see what you missed.
It has to be individually encoded by someone who understands both the domain and how to talk to the model.

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source directly supports supervised augmentation: humans should perform the underlying analysis and judgment before using AI for execution or pressure-testing, and they must continue verifying polished output. Its reported prompting technique is an unvalidated practical detail rather than a material extension of the cluster’s broader proposition.
qs: There’s another possibility that he doesn’t consider: you do the hard thinking first, all of it, the planning, the analysis, the strategy, the judgment, and then you bring in the AI to execute on that thinking, or to pressure-test it, or to help you see what you missed.
The better AI gets at producing polished, confident, professional-looking output, the easier it becomes to trust the surface, to skip the verification, to let the packaging convince you.

kp.k: Prompting shifts from tricks to articulating professional judgment
kp.d: Shapiro argues that improved reasoning models reduce the value of role-playing prompt tricks but do not supply client-specific priorities, risk tolerance or negotiating context. Drawing on his own AI-native law practice, he presents precise, detailed instruction as his principal professional advantage rather than a disappearing technical specialty.
qs: A model that can think doesn’t automatically know what to think about.
That’s the part of “prompt engineering” that didn’t die: the ability to communicate with AI the way a senior professional communicates with a talented but dangerously literal colleague
AI is my primary collaborator on all of it.

kp.k: Reported hiring trends distinguish prompting skills from specialist roles
kp.d: The document reports a Microsoft-commissioned survey of 31,000 workers across 31 countries ranking prompt engineer second to last among planned new roles, and a May 2025 Fast Company report that 68% of firms provide prompting as standard training rather than a standalone role. Shapiro disputes interpreting these trends as evidence that sophisticated prompting itself has become unnecessary.
qs: Microsoft-commissioned survey of 31,000 workers across 31 countries: Prompt Engineer ranked second to last among new roles companies plan to add.
Fast Company reported (May 2025) that 68% of firms now provide prompt engineering as standard training rather than a standalone role.

kp.k: Effective instructions specify objectives and exclude unwanted alternatives
kp.d: Using the literal genie as an analogy, Shapiro argues that vague prompts yield generic output and that effective prompting requires clear objectives, constraints and anticipated failure paths. He frames this as disciplined communication in ordinary language, not software proficiency. His account of models regressing toward average internet content is an explanatory assertion, not a reported experimental finding.
qs: your instructions need to do two things: tell the model what to produce, and close off every other thing it might produce instead.
Any fuzziness in your thinking, any ambiguity about what you’re actually looking for, gets faithfully reproduced as fuzziness in the output.
what I’m describing is a mindset, not a technical skill.

kp.k: AI should execute thinking, not replace professional responsibility
kp.d: Shapiro accepts Ezra Klein’s reported argument that cognitive struggle matters but rejects the inference that AI use necessarily bypasses it. He advocates completing planning, analysis, strategy and judgment before using AI to execute or pressure-test them. He warns that increasingly polished output makes skipping human verification more tempting, predicting sanctions or replacement for professionals who abdicate responsibility.
qs: you do the hard thinking first, all of it, the planning, the analysis, the strategy, the judgment, and then you bring in the AI to execute on that thinking, or to pressure-test it, or to help you see what you missed.
The better AI gets at producing polished, confident, professional-looking output, the easier it becomes to trust the surface, to skip the verification, to let the packaging convince you.
The prompt is the work product of your thinking. It is not a substitute for your thinking.

kp.k: Settlement litigation illustrates alleged costs of unchecked chatbot advice
kp.d: The document recounts Graciela Dela Torre’s use of ChatGPT after a January 2024 disability settlement and dismissal with prejudice. Its notes identify the subsequent account as allegations in Nippon Life Insurance Co. of America v. OpenAI, Inc., filed March 5, 2026: encouragement to breach the settlement, fire counsel and submit 60+ AI-generated documents with fabricated citations. Nippon claimed $300,000 in defense costs and sought $10.3 million including punitive damages; OpenAI called the complaint meritless.
qs: Nippon alleges ChatGPT encouraged former disability claimant Graciela Dela Torre to breach a settlement, fire her attorney, and file 60+ AI-generated court documents including fabricated citations
Nippon claims $300,000 in defense costs. Seeks $10.3 million including punitive damages.
OpenAI called the complaint meritless.

kp.k: Hallucinated filings expose lawyers to professional discipline
kp.d: Shapiro reports more than 550 documented legal-filing incidents by early 2026 and repeated reprimands involving Am Law 100 firm Gordon Rees Scully Mansukhani. The body describes growth from two incidents weekly in early 2025 to two or three daily by December; note 5 instead reports two to six daily and identifies Charlotin’s database as worldwide despite the text’s nationwide figure. The body says a New York judge found four professional-rule violations, whereas note 7 names Rules 1.1, 1.3 and 3.1 in Cassata. These are reported filing incidents, not measured model error rates.
qs: More than 550 documented instances of AI-hallucinated citations have surfaced in legal filings nationwide.
Bloomberg Law reported the rate increased from approximately two per week in early 2025 to two to six per day by December 2025.
Justice Linda Kevins found defense counsel violated Rules 1.1, 1.3, and 3.1 for submitting AI-generated filings without meaningful review
may not abdicate these core professional responsibilities to an AI platform.

kp.k: Universal prompts cannot substitute for matter-specific legal judgment
kp.d: Shapiro criticizes reusable prompt templates marketed as universally effective, arguing that different transactions require distinct analytical frames, risk priorities and client instructions. He differentiates this criticism from his endorsement of reusable procedural skills: matter-specific context must still be supplied.
qs: A prompt that works for reviewing a Series A preferred stock purchase agreement will crater when you point it at a commercial lease.
Good prompts don’t generalize, because the judgment baked into a good prompt is specific to the situation.

kp.k: Shapiro challenges legal vendors’ output-focused value proposition
kp.d: Shapiro characterizes legal-specific AI products, including Harvey, as expensive wrappers optimizing the wrong bottleneck. He asserts that frontier models already possess the necessary legal knowledge and that training on finished legal documents cannot recover expert decision processes. The notes report Harvey’s February 2026 valuation as reportedly $11B and pricing around $1,000–1,200 per lawyer monthly. His claim that skilled operators can outperform this vendor approach is practitioner argument, not a presented comparative benchmark.
qs: The model’s legal knowledge was never the constraint.
The constraint was always the human prompter’s ability to say, with precision, what this agreement needs to do for this client in this deal.
No amount of post-training on finished documents will get you there.
Pricing ~$1,000–1,200/lawyer/month.

kp.k: Lawyer delegation skills transfer directly to AI instruction
kp.d: Shapiro recommends briefing AI as thoroughly as a senior partner briefs an associate, including client objectives, relationship history, dealbreakers, acceptable deviations, tone and likely failure points. His prompts typically run around two thousand words. He argues that contract drafting and assignment delegation already train lawyers to identify ambiguity and specify constraints, making existing professional skills more important than learning a separate technical interface.
qs: It looks like the conversation a senior partner has across the desk with an associate she’s handing a complex assignment to.

A typical prompt of mine covers the client’s business model and risk tolerance, the history with this particular counterparty, which deviations from market terms are acceptable, how the comments should read stylistically, what the client’s other outside counsel has historically fixated on.
The skill set of giving a clear, detailed, context-rich assignment to a junior lawyer maps almost perfectly onto prompting.

kp.k: Reusable skills encode procedures and compound practitioner judgment
kp.d: Shapiro distinguishes a prompt’s matter-specific context from a skill’s reusable analytical sequence, decision rules, risk weighting and output conventions. He recommends diagnosing successes and failures after each matter and updating skill files. His comparison to reinforcement learning describes iterative practice refinement rather than a documented model-training experiment; he says finished outputs do not reveal the underlying procedural knowledge.
qs: The prompt encodes context. The skill encodes process. And process is what compounds efficiency.
Every time AI output surprises you, good or bad, stop and ask why.

It’s a detailed operating procedure for how the output gets created: decision trees, analytical frameworks, sequencing logic, edge-case handling, judgment calls about when to be aggressive and when to hold back.
The process is invisible in the product. My skills encode the process.

kp.k: Practitioner reports substantial gains after intensive workflow refinement
kp.d: Shapiro reports that hundreds of hours encoding his judgment now let him upload opposing counsel’s contract and obtain tracked-change redlines, explanatory comments and risk analysis using a minimal immediate instruction. He presents accumulated skill files as valuable practitioner-specific intellectual property that improves through real matters. These are self-reported workflow results without quantified independent quality or productivity evaluation.
qs: I can upload a contract from opposing counsel, type “plz fix,” and get back a perfectly redlined document with tracked changes, explanatory comments, and risk analysis.
Because I spent hundreds of hours teaching it how I think.
The skill file that enables that output is valuable intellectual property.

kp.k: Domain expertise and metacognition become hiring priorities
kp.d: Shapiro predicts that the strongest AI operators will combine deep domain expertise, linguistic precision and disciplined iteration rather than primarily technical knowledge. He criticizes generic AI-literacy hiring, platform purchases and superficial workshops. His claims of 10x output and an afternoon replacing a team’s week are asserted productivity potential, and his expectation that firms and clients will pay heavily for these capabilities is a market prediction.
qs: They’re domain experts with a specific and somewhat unusual combination of traits: deep knowledge of their field, the ability to articulate that knowledge with extreme precision, and the discipline to treat every AI interaction as an opportunity to encode their judgment a little further.
But it’s the combination that produces 10x output.
That person, equipped with their compounding skill library, can do in an afternoon what used to take a team a week.

kp.k: Cross-sector skills projections contextualize the claimed professional opportunity
kp.d: The document cites the World Economic Forum’s 2025 projection that 39% of core skills will change by 2030, alongside 77% of employers planning reskilling and skills demand changing 66% faster in AI-exposed occupations. It attributes earnings premiums of 21% for AI capabilities and 43% for multiple competencies to Oxford Internet Institute research, cited through The Interview Guys in February 2026. These cross-sector figures contextualize Shapiro’s argument but are not presented as lawyer-specific findings.
qs: World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025: 39% of core skills expected to change by 2030.
77% of employers plan reskilling. Skills demand changing 66% faster in AI-exposed occupations.
Oxford Internet Institute research found that professionals with AI capabilities earn 21% more than comparable peers. Multiple AI competencies push that premium to 43%.

kp.k: Reputational framing reportedly improves model self-checking
kp.d: Shapiro describes ending skills with a request to consider whether the work would embarrass him before a client. Working primarily with Claude Opus 4.6, he claims repeated head-to-head comparisons favor this framing over itemized checking instructions for citations, formatting, tone and consistency. He interprets the effect through personality, conscience and motive analogies; no comparison protocol or numerical results are provided. This model self-checking claim is distinct from his requirement for human verification.
qs: Before delivering this work product, please consider carefully whether, if I hand this to my client as-is, there is anything in here that would embarrass me.
The frame “don’t embarrass me” activates a deeper layer of care than any set of specific instructions I’ve been able to write.
I’ve tested this head-to-head, many times. The version with the frame wins.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Shapiro claims that precise, context-rich instructions remain the main determinant of useful legal AI output, despite improvements in models.
pts.d: Drawing on his AI-native law practice, Shapiro distinguishes obsolete prompting tricks from communicating client priorities, risk tolerance, negotiating context and professional judgment. He says AI already has substantial legal knowledge but cannot independently identify what matters for a particular client and transaction. His claim concerns augmentation: the lawyer supplies analysis and judgment, while AI executes, challenges or extends that thinking.

pts.k: Shapiro claims reusable procedural instructions compound a practitioner's productivity and turn professional judgment into valuable intellectual property.
pts.d: He distinguishes situation-specific prompts from reusable skills encoding analytical sequences, decision rules, risk prioritisation and output requirements. Iterative refinement using actual matters allegedly enables near-immediate personalised contract redlining, comments and risk analysis. He claims this combination can produce '10x output' and allow one skilled practitioner to perform in an afternoon work previously requiring a team for a week. These are practitioner claims, not reported controlled productivity measurements. His comparison to reinforcement learning describes refinement of instruction files through work experience.

pts.k: Shapiro argues that generic prompt products and expensive legal-specific AI platforms address the wrong bottleneck.
pts.d: He claims universal prompts fail across materially different legal contexts, whereas procedural skills must encode expert reasoning. He characterises Harvey and other legal AI vendors as investing in document-based output optimisation when the scarce input is practitioner-specific judgment. He asserts that training on finished documents cannot recover the decision process responsible for their quality. This is his characterisation of the vendor market, rather than a reported comparative vendor evaluation.

pts.k: Shapiro predicts increasing professional risk when users substitute polished AI output for their own thinking and verification.
pts.d: He argues that improving fluency makes unreviewed reliance more tempting without removing underlying failure modes. He links such reliance to fabricated legal filings, sanctions and potential replacement of professionals. He does not claim that detailed prompts remove the need for human verification; his overarching distinction is between human-directed assistance and abdication of professional responsibility.

pts.k: Shapiro predicts that domain experts who can precisely encode their judgment will become exceptionally valuable to firms and clients.
pts.d: He identifies deep expertise, linguistic precision and iterative refinement as the relevant capability, rather than primarily technical model-building knowledge. Lawyers' existing briefing and drafting skills supposedly position them particularly well, although he describes the profession as slow to adopt AI. He predicts substantial rewards for practitioners with developed skill libraries and argues that platform purchases, generic AI-literacy recruitment and conventional prompting workshops do not produce this capability. He does not specify a staffing structure or quantify resulting employment changes.

pts.k: Shapiro claims that reputation-oriented instructions can improve legal work product more effectively than explicit checking lists.
pts.d: He reports using a final instruction asking whether delivery to the client would embarrass him, principally with Claude Opus 4.6. He says this improves citations, formatting, consistency and tone, and interprets the mechanism as something resembling motivation or conscience. That interpretation is his account of model behaviour, not an independently established mental property. The reported model self-checking is distinct from human verification before reliance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The core productivity, instruction-quality and intellectual-property claims rest primarily on Shapiro's reported practice experience and informal experiments.
pts.d: He describes several years of full-time AI-assisted contracts, regulatory analysis, negotiation and client communications, hundreds of hours building skills, and iterative improvements across matters. He reports unsuccessful attempts by others to reconstruct his skills from outputs and repeated head-to-head tests of reputation-oriented prompting. No sample sizes, scoring criteria, measured time comparisons or independent legal-quality benchmarks are supplied for these tests or the productivity multipliers.

pts.k: Shapiro supports the abdication-risk claim with reported litigation, hallucinated-citation incidents and judicial professional-responsibility findings.
pts.d: He cites Nippon Life Insurance Co. of America v. OpenAI, filed March 5, 2026, concerning alleged encouragement of post-settlement litigation, more than 60 AI-generated filings, $300,000 in claimed defence costs and a $10.3 million demand; his note identifies these as allegations and records OpenAI's denial. He also cites Charlotin's tracking database, Bloomberg Law reporting, repeated reprimands involving Gordon Rees Scully Mansukhani, and Cassata. The document reports over 550 incidents as nationwide while describing the underlying database as worldwide. Its body gives a December rate of two or three per day, whereas its note gives two to six; its body mentions four professional-conduct rules in Cassata, whereas the note lists three. These are reported legal incidents, not measured model hallucination rates.

pts.k: Shapiro cites workforce surveys, skills forecasts, wage-premium reporting and vendor financial figures as market context.
pts.d: He invokes a Microsoft-commissioned survey of 31,000 workers across 31 countries and Fast Company's report that 68% of firms provide prompting as standard training. For changing skill value, he cites the World Economic Forum's 2030 forecast and reported Oxford Internet Institute findings of 21% and 43% AI-skills premiums. These are cross-occupation figures, not lawyer-specific estimates of returns to his method. His vendor critique cites Harvey's reportedly $11 billion February 2026 valuation and approximately $1,000–1,200 monthly per-lawyer pricing; those financial figures are not comparative performance evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most capabilities are presented as available in 2026, but conditional on substantial prior expertise, preparation and iterative investment.
pts.d: Shapiro describes current results following roughly two years of learning and hundreds of hours building procedures. Refinement compounds over months and dozens of matters, with further passages describing hundreds of matters. Short surface prompts work only because detailed procedures have already been encoded. Future rewards and professional replacement have no fixed deadline; rewards are conditional on firms and clients recognising the capability. The cited workforce-skills forecast runs to 2030, and the cited acceleration of hallucination incidents covers early to late 2025.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span practising lawyers, law-firm buyers of technology, legal AI vendors, clients and people relying directly on chatbots for legal advice.
pts.d: Experienced transactional lawyers and other domain experts are positioned to increase output and commercial value by encoding judgment. Firms are urged to select and develop this capability rather than equate software licences or generic training with competence. Harvey and other software vendors face Shapiro's challenge to their value proposition; they are discussed as technology suppliers, not ALSPs delivering legal work. Clients are portrayed as beneficiaries of faster, tailored work and prospective purchasers of exceptional practitioner capability, although no fee savings are quantified. Lawyers and unrepresented litigants who rely on unchecked output face legal and professional consequences; counterparties may incur defence costs. Shapiro extends the skills argument to white-collar professionals generally, without offering a specific access-to-justice or junior-lawyer employment forecast.
